def: A group of inherited collagen defects causing hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints and fragile blood vessels, with vascular and joint complications.
Forced exhalation against a closed airway, which raises chest pressure and lowers venous return. It increases the murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and decreases most others.
Kidney disease with heavy proteinuria (over 3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia. Caused by podocyte or basement membrane damage, as in minimal change disease.
Generalized dysfunction of the proximal renal tubule, wasting glucose, amino acids, phosphate and bicarbonate, producing type 2 renal tubular acidosis.
Neuroendocrine cells of the adrenal medulla that release epinephrine and norepinephrine. Pheochromocytoma arises from them.
Flushing, diarrhea, wheezing and right-sided valvular heart disease from serotonin released by a carcinoid tumor, usually after liver metastasis. Urine 5-HIAA is elevated.
The most common pediatric kidney cancer, with blastemal, stromal and epithelial elements. Presents as a large flank mass; linked to WT1 deletion and WAGR syndrome.
Cells lining the seminiferous tubules that nurture developing sperm cells, secrete inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone, and form the blood-testis barrier. They respond to FSH.
Antibodies against type IV collagen of the basement membranes of the glomerulus and alveolus cause rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with lung hemorrhage. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG.
Episodic vasospasm of the fingers or toes causing white, then blue, then red color changes with cold. Secondary forms are linked to scleroderma and lupus.
A small-vessel vasculitis occurring with asthma, eosinophilia and nasal polyps, often p-ANCA positive.
A test for antibodies on red cells. Direct detects antibodies bound to a patient's cells (autoimmune hemolysis); indirect detects antibodies in serum (transfusion matching, Rh incompatibility).
Round, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of aggregated alpha-synuclein in neurons. They are the hallmark of Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.
An immune reaction to gluten that damages the small intestine villi, causing malabsorption. Associated with anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 and dermatitis herpetiformis.
Large binucleate cells with owl-eye nucleoli, the diagnostic cells of Hodgkin lymphoma. They are CD15 and CD30 positive.
An embryonic outpouching of the oral ectoderm that forms the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis). Remnants can give rise to craniopharyngioma.
A sporadic neurocutaneous disorder with a facial port-wine stain in the V1 distribution, leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures and glaucoma, from a GNAQ mutation.
Hepatic vein thrombosis causing congestive liver disease: hepatomegaly, ascites and abdominal pain. Associated with polycythemia vera and hypercoagulable states.
A growth disorder from abnormal imprinting at 11p15, with macroglossia, omphalocele, hypoglycemia and a risk of Wilms tumor.
Anemia where iron-loaded mitochondria ring the red cell nucleus (ring sideroblasts) because heme synthesis is impaired. Caused by ALAS2 mutations, alcohol, lead and isoniazid.
Dendritic antigen-presenting cells of the epidermis. They contain Birbeck granules and are the cell of origin in Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
Infection with Trypanosoma cruzi spread by reduviid (kissing) bugs. Chronic disease causes dilated cardiomyopathy, megacolon and megaesophagus; acute disease can show Romana sign.
Testicular interstitial cells that make testosterone in response to LH. They contain Reinke crystals.
A trisomy 18 disorder causing severe intellectual disability, rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, micrognathia and heart defects. Most infants die within the first year.
A 47,XXY disorder with small firm testes, tall stature, gynecomastia and infertility from hypergonadism with high FSH and LH. A Barr body is present.
Pre-excitation via an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) bypassing the AV node. The ECG shows a short PR interval and delta wave; risk of tachyarrhythmia.
Autosomal recessive defect of the distal tubule Na-Cl cotransporter, mimicking thiazide use. Causes hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria.
X-linked HGPRT deficiency in purine salvage, causing hyperuricemia, gout, self-mutilation, dystonia and intellectual disability.
Trisomy 13, causing holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly and heart defects. Most infants die in the first year.
Pituitary necrosis after postpartum hemorrhage. Causes inability to lactate, amenorrhea and hypopituitarism.
The most common inherited bleeding disorder, from deficient or defective von Willebrand factor. Causes mucosal bleeding with prolonged bleeding time and aPTT.
Autosomal recessive defect of the thick ascending limb Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, mimicking loop diuretic use. Causes hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis and hypercalciuria.
A lysosomal storage disease from sphingomyelinase deficiency. Features hepatosplenomegaly, foam cells, a cherry-red macula and neurodegeneration.
Anemia from premature destruction of red blood cells, with raised reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin and LDH, and low haptoglobin.
A prion disease causing rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus and spongiform change in the brain. EEG shows periodic sharp waves.
Transmural rupture of the esophagus from forceful vomiting. Causes chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema and mediastinitis.
Infection with Tropheryma whipplei causing malabsorption, arthralgia and neurologic symptoms. Biopsy shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages.
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children aged 4 to 8, presenting with hip pain and a limp.
A murmur lasting the whole of systole, seen in mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation and ventricular septal defect.
Intrauterine adhesions (scarring) following uterine curettage or infection, causing amenorrhea or hypomenorrhea and infertility.
Autosomal dominant overactivity of the collecting duct sodium channel (ENaC), causing hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with low renin and aldosterone.
A mucopolysaccharidosis from alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency. Causes coarse facies, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly and intellectual disability.
Round, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of aggregated alpha-synuclein in neurons. They are the hallmark of Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.
Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury causing the waiter's tip posture: arm adducted, internally rotated and extended. Often follows shoulder dystocia.
Vaginal epithelial cells covered with bacteria, giving them a stippled border. They are diagnostic of bacterial vaginosis.
Ovarian stromal cells that make androgens in response to LH, which granulosa cells convert to estrogen.
Ovarian follicle cells that surround the oocyte, convert androgens to estrogen using aromatase under FSH, and later form the corpus luteum.
An X-linked dominant MECP2 disorder in girls. After normal early development, loss of purposeful hand use, hand-wringing, seizures and regression occur.
Acute encephalopathy with fatty liver in children given aspirin during a viral illness (influenza, varicella).
The inferior frontal gyrus region (Brodmann 44, 45) that produces speech. Damage causes nonfluent aphasia with intact comprehension.
A numbered region of the cerebral cortex defined by its cell layout, such as area 4 (primary motor cortex).
An outpouching of the pharyngeal wall above the upper esophageal sphincter, causing dysphagia, halitosis and regurgitation of undigested food.
An X-linked immunodeficiency with eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections. Caused by a WAS gene mutation.
Ovarian follicle cells that surround the oocyte, convert androgens to estrogen using aromatase under FSH, and later form the corpus luteum.
An autosomal recessive DNA repair defect causing pancytopenia, short stature, radial limb defects and cancer risk.
An X-linked defect in type IV collagen causing hematuria, hearing loss and eye abnormalities. Electron microscopy shows a basket-weave glomerular basement membrane.
An X-linked defect in copper transport (ATP7A) causing kinky hair, hypotonia and neurodegeneration in male infants.
Thromboangiitis obliterans, inflammation of small and medium vessels of the extremities in smokers. Causes digital ischemia and claudication.
Reversal of a left-to-right cardiac shunt to right-to-left due to pulmonary hypertension, causing late cyanosis and clubbing.
Glycogen storage disease type I from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency. Causes severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis and gout.
Glycogen storage disease type II from lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Causes cardiomegaly, hypotonia and early death in infants.
The fluid-filled space between the glomerular capillaries and Bowman capsule, which receives the glomerular filtrate.
X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causing buildup of ceramide trihexoside. Features angiokeratomas, burning limb pain and kidney failure.
Lysosomal galactocerebrosidase deficiency causing globoid cells, optic atrophy and demyelination with neurodegeneration in infants.
Anemia with large red cells and hypersegmented neutrophils, from impaired DNA synthesis due to folate or vitamin B12 deficiency.
Amnestic disorder from thiamine deficiency in chronic alcohol use, with anterograde amnesia and confabulation. Follows Wernicke encephalopathy.
Pancytopenia from bone marrow failure with an empty, fatty marrow. Causes include drugs, viruses and radiation.
The posterior superior temporal gyrus responsible for language comprehension. Damage causes fluent, nonsensical speech with poor comprehension.
Lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) injury causing claw hand and sometimes Horner syndrome, often from traction on the arm.
A peroxisomal disorder of phytanic acid breakdown causing retinitis pigmentosa, ataxia, neuropathy and ichthyosis.
A 0-10 assessment of a newborn at 1 and 5 minutes, scoring appearance, pulse, grimace, activity and respiration.
Testicular interstitial cells that make testosterone in response to LH. They contain Reinke crystals.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia from defective dynein arms. Causes situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis and infertility.
Pericarditis and fever weeks after myocardial infarction, thought to be autoimmune.
A paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure on inspiration. Seen in constrictive pericarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Inherited defect of platelet GpIb, so platelets cannot bind von Willebrand factor. Causes giant platelets, thrombocytopenia and bleeding.
The most common inherited bleeding disorder, from deficient or defective von Willebrand factor. Causes mucosal bleeding with prolonged bleeding time and aPTT.
Clumps of denatured hemoglobin within red cells, seen in G6PD deficiency. They are removed by splenic macrophages to form bite cells.
Glycogen storage disease type III from debranching enzyme deficiency, causing fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly with normal lactate.
Glomerular inflammation with hematuria, red cell casts, hypertension, azotemia and mild proteinuria. Seen in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and IgA nephropathy.
X-linked iduronate sulfatase deficiency, a mucopolysaccharidosis. Similar to Hurler but with no corneal clouding and aggressive behavior.
An autosomal recessive defect in neutral amino acid transport (tryptophan), causing pellagra-like symptoms.
Congenital pure red cell aplasia presenting in infancy with macrocytic anemia, short stature and thumb abnormalities.
Dorsal midbrain syndrome with impaired upward gaze, convergence-retraction nystagmus and pupillary light-near dissociation. Often due to a pineal tumor.
The most numerous neurons of the cerebellar cortex. They use glutamate as an excitatory transmitter and send parallel fibers to Purkinje cells.
Large inhibitory GABAergic neurons of the cerebellar cortex whose axons are the sole output of the cortex.
Longitudinal mucosal tears at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful vomiting, causing hematemesis, classically in alcohol use.
Skin that sloughs off with lateral pressure. Positive in pemphigus vulgaris, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
A tunnel at the wrist where the ulnar nerve and artery pass. Compression causes hand weakness and numbness of the fifth finger.
Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction: marked colonic dilation without a mechanical blockage, usually in hospitalized or post-surgical patients.
Inflammation of the tibial tuberosity from overuse in adolescent athletes, causing knee pain below the patella.
A defect of GnRH neuron migration causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia (absent sense of smell). Low GnRH, LH and FSH lead to delayed puberty.
A trisomy 18 disorder causing severe intellectual disability, rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, micrognathia and heart defects. Most infants die within the first year.
A peroxisome biogenesis disorder causing hypotonia, liver dysfunction, craniofacial abnormalities and early death.
Loss of the maternal UBE3A gene on chromosome 15. Features severe developmental delay, ataxia, seizures and inappropriate laughter.
An inherited sodium channel disorder with ST elevation in V1-V3 on ECG, causing risk of sudden death from ventricular fibrillation.
WT1 mutation causing early-onset nephropathy, gonadal dysgenesis and Wilms tumor.
IgA nephropathy, with IgA deposition in the glomerular mesangium and hematuria after mucosal infection.
An autosomal dominant VHL tumor suppressor loss causing hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.
Thiamine deficiency in alcohol use, with Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) that may progress to Korsakoff amnesia.
Anemia with large red cells and hypersegmented neutrophils, from impaired DNA synthesis due to folate or vitamin B12 deficiency.
Remnants of nuclear DNA in red cells, normally removed by the spleen. They suggest asplenia or hyposplenism.
Upward movement of the great toe with fanning of the other toes on plantar stroking, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion in adults.
Spinal cord hemisection causing ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration and proprioception, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion.
Spinal muscular atrophy type 1, from SMN1 loss causing lower motor neuron degeneration. Presents with floppy infants and tongue fasciculations.
A midbrain atrophy pattern on sagittal MRI, characteristic of progressive supranuclear palsy.
An inherited peripheral neuropathy causing distal muscle wasting, foot deformities (high arches) and sensory loss, often from PMP22 duplication.
Deficiency of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase causing unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Type I is severe with kernicterus.
Benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia from defective bilirubin excretion (MRP2), with a black liver.
Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons, found in rabies.
Relief of testicular pain on elevating the scrotum, suggesting epididymitis rather than torsion.
Small follicle-like structures with eosinophilic fluid seen in granulosa cell tumors.
Loss of the paternal chromosome 15q11-q13 region. Features hypotonia, hyperphagia with obesity, hypogonadism and intellectual disability.
Autosomal recessive long QT syndrome with congenital sensorineural deafness.
Autosomal dominant long QT syndrome without deafness, predisposing to torsades de pointes.
Nonciliated bronchiolar cells that secrete protective proteins, detoxify substances and serve as progenitor cells.
A lung apex tumor that compresses the sympathetic chain and brachial plexus, causing Horner syndrome and arm pain.
Tissue cells containing histamine granules that mediate type I hypersensitivity reactions via IgE.
Idiopathic acute facial nerve (CN VII) paralysis affecting the upper and lower face on one side. Usually resolves, and is treated with steroids.
Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension and repetition, from a lesion of Wernicke area.
Impaired repetition with fluent speech and intact comprehension, from lesion of the arcuate fasciculus.
Loss of both language production and comprehension, from a large left hemisphere lesion.
Frontotemporal dementia with Pick bodies and frontotemporal atrophy, causing personality change and disinhibition.
A remnant of the vitelline duct forming a pouch in the ileum. May contain ectopic gastric tissue and cause painless bleeding.
Autosomal dominant STK11 mutation with hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, with increased cancer risk.
Migratory venous thrombosis (thrombophlebitis) as a paraneoplastic sign, classically with pancreatic cancer and other adenocarcinomas.
A factitious disorder where a person falsifies illness to gain medical attention.
Benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a normal liver, similar to Dubin-Johnson syndrome.
Hyper-IgE syndrome with recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses, coarse facies, retained baby teeth and eczema, from impaired TH17 cells.
An autoimmune disease with arterial and venous clots and recurrent miscarriage, due to antiphospholipid antibodies.
Autosomal dominant germline TP53 mutation predisposing to sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors and leukemia.
Raised pressure within a closed muscle compartment compromising perfusion. Presents with pain on passive stretch, tense swelling and paresthesia.
A clinical prediction rule estimating the probability of pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis.
Epidemic pleurodynia caused by coxsackie B virus, with sudden severe chest or abdominal pain and fever.
A list of medications potentially harmful in older adults, used to guide prescribing.
Perihepatitis from pelvic inflammatory disease (chlamydia, gonorrhea), causing right upper quadrant pain with violin-string adhesions.
Primary hyperaldosteronism, usually from an adrenal adenoma. Causes hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with low renin.
Cells lining the seminiferous tubules that nurture developing sperm cells, secrete inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone, and form the blood-testis barrier. They respond to FSH.
Lipid-laden macrophages with a bubbly cytoplasm, seen in atherosclerotic plaques and lipid storage diseases.
A defect of GnRH neuron migration causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia (absent sense of smell). Low GnRH, LH and FSH lead to delayed puberty.
An inactivated X chromosome seen as a dense mass in the nucleus of female cells.
Excess serotonergic activity (e.g., from SSRIs with MAOIs) causing hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation and diarrhea.
Painful, raised nodules on the finger or toe pads in infective endocarditis, from immune complex deposition.
Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease: asthma, nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity.
Storage granules in endothelial cells holding von Willebrand factor and P-selectin.
Glycogen storage disease type VI from liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, with mild fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.
Antibody-secreting cells derived from B cells, with an eccentric nucleus and clock-face chromatin. They proliferate in multiple myeloma.
Upward movement of the great toe with fanning of the other toes on plantar stroking, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion in adults.
Nonfluent speech with intact comprehension and impaired repetition, from lesion of Broca area.
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, an autosomal dominant disease with mucocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent nosebleeds and arteriovenous malformations.
A palpable, nontender gallbladder with jaundice, suggesting malignant bile duct obstruction such as pancreatic head cancer.
Functional kidney failure in advanced liver disease with ascites, from renal vasoconstriction. The kidneys are histologically normal.
A hernia through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament, more common in women, with a high risk of strangulation.
Thymoma with hypogammaglobulinemia, leading to recurrent infections.
CD4-positive T lymphocytes that coordinate immune responses by secreting cytokines. They include Th1, Th2 and Th17 subsets.
Episodic vasospasm of the fingers or toes causing white, then blue, then red color changes with cold. Secondary forms are linked to scleroderma and lupus.
A clinical prediction rule estimating the probability of pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis.
Intranuclear viral inclusions seen in herpesvirus infections (HSV, VZV, CMV).
A squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound, burn scar or sinus tract.
Small white spots on the buccal mucosa, an early sign of measles.
Autosomal recessive DNA helicase (BLM) defect causing short stature, sun-sensitive facial rash and increased cancers.
An embryonic outpouching of the oral ectoderm that forms the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis). Remnants can give rise to craniopharyngioma.
Facial twitching when the facial nerve is tapped in front of the ear, a sign of hypocalcemia.
Carpal spasm induced by inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for minutes, indicating hypocalcemia.
Nodular glomerulosclerosis from diabetic nephropathy, with mesangial matrix expansion in the glomeruli.
Acute adrenal failure from bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, classically in meningococcal sepsis.
Growth of an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease, with hyperpigmentation.
Growth hormone insensitivity from a GH receptor mutation. Short stature with high GH and low IGF-1.
Squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the skin, presenting as a scaly red plaque.
A fibroepithelial breast tumor with leaf-like projections and a cellular stroma, usually benign but may recur.
Inactivated X chromosomes seen as dense nuclear masses in female cells.
A 7q11.23 deletion including elastin. Features elfin facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia and an outgoing personality.
Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing in response to raised intracranial pressure.
Ventilated lung volume that does not take part in gas exchange. Anatomic dead space is the conducting airways; physiologic dead space adds ventilated but unperfused alveoli.
A neuroendocrine tumor, most often in the small bowel or lung, that secretes serotonin. Causes carcinoid syndrome after liver metastasis.
Nonciliated bronchiolar cells that secrete protective proteins and serve as progenitors.
Red cells with a central dark spot surrounded by a pale ring, seen in thalassemia, liver disease and hemoglobin C disease.
Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia from autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor, causing megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms.
Upward movement of the great toe with fanning of the other toes on plantar stroking, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion in adults.
Loss of balance when standing with feet together and eyes closed, indicating a proprioceptive (dorsal column) or vestibular deficit.
The acute disseminated form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis in infants, with rash, organ involvement and fever.
Painful, shallow oral ulcers with a yellow base and red halo; recurrent canker sores.
Familial adenomatous polyposis with osteomas, soft tissue tumors and dental abnormalities. APC gene mutation.
